Reproductive investment in the bluespotted hind Cephalopholis cyanostigma was examined through field collections conducted in the central Great Barrier Reef. Histological analysis of gonadal tissue showed a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 3% [GSI = 3%] at a water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This value is consistent with an iteroparous spawning strategy in which gamete production is concentrated into discrete seasonal events rather than maintained continuously throughout the year. Furthermore, size-at-age data from otolith readings provided estimates of key life-history parameters, including the total length at which 50% of females are reproductively mature. That length was determined to be 23 centimeters [Lp = 23 centimeters], a figure that aligns well with published values for other small-bodied epinephelids inhabiting similar coral reef environments within the Indo-Pacific region.

The relationship between length and somatic mass in Cephalopholis cyanostigma was derived from a large specimen series encompassing the full size range encountered during surveys. Using the length–weight conversion established for this species, the wet weight of a female at the onset of sexual maturity was estimated at 175 grams [Wwp = 175 grams], a value reflecting the accumulation of sufficient somatic reserves to support vitellogenesis and subsequent spawning. The maximum recorded total length observed in the field population was 55 centimeters [Li = 55 centimeters], representing the upper limit of somatic growth for this species in its natural habitat. At this asymptotic size, the corresponding ultimate wet weight was calculated to be 2432 grams [Wwi = 2432 grams], placing the bluespotted hind among the smaller members of the genus Cephalopholis, a group typically characterized by moderate adult body sizes and relatively fast individual growth rates.

Early life-history traits of the bluespotted hind were investigated using laboratory-reared progeny obtained from strip-spawned gametes. Fertilised eggs, which are pelagic and transparent, were incubated at a stable temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C] until eclosion, which occurred after approximately 7.5 days [ab = approximately 7.5 days]. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae were extremely small, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.000449 grams [Wwb = 0.000449 grams], a value derived directly from the measured egg diameter of 0.95 millimeters using the standard volumetric formula for a spherical teleost egg. This minute initial mass underscores the high degree of larval vulnerability during the early planktonic phase, matching the typical pattern observed among small-bodied serranids that produce numerous small, pelagic eggs. The hatchlings remained endotrophic for the first few days, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding.

Lifespan estimation for Cephalopholis cyanostigma was based on recapture data from a long-term tagging study conducted on a protected reef system. The maximum longevity recorded in the field was 35 years [am = 35 years], a surprisingly high value for a relatively small grouper species, suggesting that this hind exhibits an unusually slow pace of life compared to many other serranids of comparable adult body size at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This extended lifespan, observed at an average ambient water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], indicates that the species may possess effective cellular maintenance mechanisms or experience very low natural adult mortality rates within its coral reef habitat. The maximum age is likely facilitated by the species' cryptic, shelter-associated behaviour, which reduces predation risk. Comparable longevity values have been documented in other long-lived tropical reef fishes such as certain lutjanids, though such extended lifespans are rare among fishes of the 55-centimeter maximum length class.

Reproduction in this hind is characterised by a protracted spawning season rather than a single intense pulse, which spreads energetic investment across several months. The pronounced difference between the 175-gram mass at sexual maturity (175 grams) [Wwp = 175 grams] and the 2432-gram ultimate body mass (2432 grams) [Wwi = 2432 grams] suggests that females continue to invest substantially in somatic growth well after reaching puberty, a strategy that may enhance lifetime fecundity by allowing larger, more fecund spawners to dominate later reproductive seasons. This growth pattern is consistent with the species' long maximum lifespan, as the energetic trade-off between immediate reproduction and continued body growth is shifted toward the latter, enabling individuals to reach a relatively large ultimate size and thereby maximise cumulative reproductive output over a long adult life.
